results.content:
Claude Cowork isn’t trying to be clever or viral. It’s designed around folders, documents, and bounded access — the boring stuff that real work depends on. Justin sees this as the clearest signal yet that Anthropic is building for companies, not mass consumers. Frank agrees the approach makes sense, even if the price limits who it’s for. The bigger insight: OpenAI and Anthropic are no longer chasing the same users, or even solving the same problems.

### Hyper-personalisation is powerful — and uncomfortable for good reason [...] Frank: Yeah.

Justin: Like, there’s no need for it. And Plus specifically, you’re paying money to get straight to the truth. You don’t need, you know, that seems like a kind of a social contract thing that you’re breaking. If I was able to pay, like you can do it within Google already with YouTube. So, and that’s actually exactly the parallel. In YouTube you can pay a tenner a month to not see ads. And so the same thing is in Google. I should be able to pay 20 quid a month to not see ads. Now, if you start putting ads in there, you’ve broken our contract.

Frank: Which in a way, I think what you’re pointing out would say to me that, yeah, the roadmap will definitely be this. This will come to Plus and there’ll be a Plus Plus tier. There’ll be a Plus ads-free tier as well. [...] ## Key insights from the podcast

### Ads don’t just change the business model — they risk changing the answers

The concern with ads in ChatGPT isn’t just that people dislike marketing. It’s that once advertising exists, the system has an incentive to optimise for visibility and influence, not accuracy. Justin’s worry is structural: models could slowly learn to favour sponsored outcomes, just as search engines did. Frank’s unease is more subtle — ads interacting with memory could create long-term distortions in how the AI “understands” user preferences. Even with promises of separation, unintended consequences are hard to avoid.

### Claude Cowork shows a clear split between consumer AI and work AI

results.title: Claude is a space to think | Anthropic \ Anthropic
results.content:
Even ads that don’t directly influence an AI model’s responses and instead appear separately within the chat window would compromise what we want Claude to be: a clear space to think and work. Such ads would also introduce an incentive to optimize for engagement—for the amount of time people spend using Claude and how often they return. These metrics aren’t necessarily aligned with being genuinely helpful. The most useful AI interaction might be a short one, or one that resolves the user’s request without prompting further conversation. [...] # Claude is a space to think

Claude is a space to think

There are many good places for advertising. A conversation with Claude is not one of them.

Advertising drives competition, helps people discover new products, and allows services like email and social media to be offered for free. We’ve run our own ad campaigns, and our AI models have, in turn, helped many of our customers in the advertising industry.

But including ads in conversations with Claude would be incompatible with what we want Claude to be: a genuinely helpful assistant for work and for deep thinking. [...] Our analysis of conversations with Claude (conducted in a way that keeps all data private and anonymous) shows that an appreciable portion involve topics that are sensitive or deeply personal—the kinds of conversations you might have with a trusted advisor. Many other uses involve complex software engineering tasks, deep work, or thinking through difficult problems. The appearance of ads in these contexts would feel incongruous—and, in many cases, inappropriate.
